questions.stemText:
An alternating p.d. is applied across the Y-plates of a cathode-ray-oscilloscope (CRO) and produces the trace shown below. The peak voltage of the alternating p.d. is 2.8 V and its frequency is 50 Hz.

[Sinusoidal trace across a grid six divisions wide and four divisions high. Three full cycles are shown and each peak is about 1.4 divisions above the central horizontal line.]

What are the time-base and Y-gain settings of the CRO?

Option | time-base / $\mathrm{ms\,div^{-1}}$ | Y-gain / $\mathrm{V\,div^{-1}}$
A | 10 | 1.0
B | 20 | 1.0
C | 10 | 2.0
D | 20 | 2.0

stemImage.alt: Question 26: An alternating p.d. is applied across the Y-plates of a cathode-ray-oscilloscope (CRO) and produces the trace shown below. The peak voltage of the alternating p

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Each setting follows from dividing a known quantity by its span on the trace.
questions.misconception: Confusing peak with peak-to-peak height

explanation.body: The period is $T=1/f=1/50=0.020\ \mathrm{s}$ and spans two horizontal divisions, giving a time-base of $10\ \mathrm{ms\,div^{-1}}$. The $2.8\ \mathrm{V}$ peak spans 1.4 vertical divisions, so the Y-gain is $2.8/1.4=2.0\ \mathrm{V\,div^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the peak-to-peak height with the peak voltage.
perOption.B: Uses a half-cycle for the period and the peak-to-peak height for the peak voltage.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a half-cycle for the period.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
When an alternating current, $I=I_0\cos\omega t$, passes through a resistor, the mean power dissipated in the resistor is $P$.

The peak value of the alternating current is then reduced by half and the current is passed through a diode.

What is the mean power dissipated in the resistor in terms of $P$?

A $P/8$
B $P/4$
C $P/2$
D $P$

stemImage.alt: Question 25: When an alternating current, I = I0 cos t, passes through a resistor, the mean power dissipated in the resistor is P. The peak value of the alternating current

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Two distinct changes to the average power must be combined.
questions.misconception: Treating power as proportional to current

explanation.body: At each instant, the resistor dissipates power $I^2R$, so halving the current amplitude reduces the mean power to $P/4$ before rectification. An ideal diode removes one of the two equal contributions from the half-cycles, giving a mean power of $P/8$ over a full cycle.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Accounts for halving the current amplitude but ignores the blocked half-cycle.
perOption.C: Accounts for the blocked half-cycle alone.
perOption.D: Leaves the mean power unchanged despite the reduced current amplitude and the blocked half-cycle.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An alternating potential with a saw tooth waveform is shown below.

What is the root-mean-square voltage of the waveform?
questions.stemText: An alternating potential with a saw tooth waveform is shown below. V/V V0 t −V0 What is the root-mean-square voltage of the waveform? A 0 B V 0 3 C V 0 2 D V 0

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must square and average a non-sinusoidal waveform before taking the square root.
questions.misconception: Using the sinusoidal RMS factor for any alternating voltage

explanation.body: Over the first half-period, $V(t)=(2V_0/T)t$, and the other half has the same mean square. Thus $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{T}\int_0^{T/2}\frac{4V_0^2}{T^2}t^2\,dt}$. Evaluating gives $\sqrt{\frac{8V_0^2}{T^3}\frac{T^3}{3\times8}}=\frac{V_0}{\sqrt3}$.

perOption.A: Uses the average voltage, which is zero.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the RMS value for a sinusoidal waveform.
perOption.D: Uses the RMS value for an alternating voltage of constant magnitude $V_0$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two wires, X and Y, are made from the same metal. The diameter of wire Y is twice that of wire X.

Both wires are connected in series to a battery as shown.

[A single loop contains a battery across the top and wire X followed by the thicker wire Y along the bottom.]

What is the ratio $\frac{\text{average drift speed of free electrons in wire Y}}{\text{average drift speed of free electrons in wire X}}$?

A. 0.25
B. 0.50
C. 2.0
D. 4.0

stemImage.alt: Question 21: Two wires, X and Y, are made from the same metal. The diameter of wire Y is twice that of wire X. Both wires are connected in series to a battery as shown. What

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students apply the current equation and square the diameter ratio to obtain the area ratio.
questions.misconception: Using diameter instead of cross-sectional area

explanation.body: From $I=nevA$, the drift speed is $v=I/(neA)$. Since $I$, $n$ and $e$ are the same for both wires, $v\propto1/A\propto1/d^2$. Hence $v_Y/v_X=d_X^2/d_Y^2=d^2/(2d)^2=0.25$.

perOption.A: Correct. Quadrupling the area quarters the drift speed.
perOption.B: Uses inverse diameter instead of inverse cross-sectional area.
perOption.C: Treats drift speed as directly proportional to diameter.
perOption.D: Treats drift speed as directly proportional to cross-sectional area.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An alternating square wave power supply V is connected to a resistor of resistance R and a diode in the circuit as shown.

The variation of V with time t is shown in the graph.

What is the mean power dissipated in the resistor?
questions.stemText: An alternating square wave power supply V is connected to a resistor of resistance R and a diode in the circuit as shown. The variation of V with time t is shown in the graph. What is the mean power dissipated in the resistor? A V 2 R 0 4 B V 2 R 0 2 C V 2 0 2 R D V 2 R 0

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must account for diode conduction over half the cycle before finding the RMS voltage and power.
questions.misconception: Squaring the mean voltage instead of taking the mean square

explanation.body: The diode rectifies the square wave so the resistor sees $V_0$ for half a period $T$ and zero for the other half. Thus $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{V_0^2(T/2)/T}=V_0/\sqrt{2}$. The mean power is $P_{\mathrm{ave}}=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R=V_0^2/(2R)$.

perOption.A: Squares the mean voltage $V_0/2$ rather than taking the mean of the squared voltage.
perOption.B: Correct. The resistor dissipates peak power for half the cycle.
perOption.C: Applies the RMS factor $1/\sqrt{2}$ to only one of the two voltage factors in the power calculation.
perOption.D: Treats the resistor as dissipating peak power throughout the cycle.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A torch is switched on and left until its battery is flat. During this time, the current in the lamp remains steady at $0.60\ \mathrm{A}$ for three hours and then decreases uniformly to zero in the next hour. What is the total charge passing through the lamp? A $1.2 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{C}$ B $4.3 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{C}$ C $7.6 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{C}$ D $8.6 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{C}$

stemImage.alt: Question 21: A torch is switched on and left until its battery is flat. During this time, the current in the lamp remains steady at 0.60 A for three hours and then decreases

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two-stage charge calculation: constant current plus a linearly falling current (area of a triangle).
questions.misconception: Forgetting to convert hours to seconds or treating the falling stage as full current

explanation.body: Current is $I=dQ/dt$. In the first three hours, $Q=(0.60)(3\times60\times60)=6480\ \mathrm{C}$. In the fourth hour the mean current is half the initial current, giving $Q=\tfrac12(0.60)(60\times60)=1080\ \mathrm{C}$. The total is $6480+1080\approx7.6\times10^3\ \mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Uses a time scale of minutes without converting it to seconds.
perOption.B: Uses the fourth-hour mean current for all four hours.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Keeps the current at 0.60 A throughout the fourth hour.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
When a fixed resistor is connected across an a.c. source of peak voltage 150 V, the power dissipated is 13 W. Two such fixed resistors are now connected in series to the electrical mains of 240 V r.m.s.

What is the total power dissipated in the resistors?
questions.stemText: When a fixed resistor is connected across an a.c. source of peak voltage 150 V, the power dissipated is 13 W. Two such fixed resistors are now connected in series to the electrical mains of 240 V r.m.s. What is the total power dissipated in the resistors? A 17 W B 33 W C 47 W D 67 W

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert the first voltage to r.m.s., infer one resistance, and use the series total.
questions.misconception: Mixing peak and r.m.s. voltages

explanation.body: The first source gives $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=150/\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V}$. Using $P=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R$ gives $13=150^2/(2R)$, so $R=865\ \Omega$ and the series resistance is $2\times865\ \Omega$. The total power is $240^2/(2\times865)\approx33\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Treating the first peak voltage as r.m.s. doubles the inferred resistance and halves the final power.
perOption.B: Correct. The series pair dissipates 33 W.
perOption.C: The calculation requires the square of the r.m.s. voltage divided by the full series resistance.
perOption.D: This applies the full mains voltage to just one resistor.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Free electrons flow along a copper wire X of radius $5.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}$ with an average drift speed of $2.8\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The current in the wire is $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

There is a current of $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ in a copper wire Y of radius $1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}$.

What is the average drift speed of the free electrons in copper wire Y?

A $4.7\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
B $9.3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
C $1.1\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
D $1.9\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: Free electrons flow along a copper wire X of radius 5.0  10–5 m with an average drift speed of 2.8  10–2 m s–1. The current in the wire is 3.0 A. There is a c

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding carrier density first and applying it to a wire with a different cross-sectional area.
questions.misconception: Scaling drift speed by radius instead of cross-sectional area.

explanation.body: For wire X, $n=I/(vAq)=3.0/[(2.8\times10^{-2})\pi(5.0\times10^{-5})^2(1.6\times10^{-19})]=8.526\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Both wires are copper, so they have the same free-electron number density. For wire Y, $v=I/(nAq)=2.0/[(8.526\times10^{28})\pi(1.0\times10^{-4})^2(1.6\times10^{-19})]=4.7\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats twice the radius as twice the area, though the area increases fourfold.
perOption.C: Underestimates the effect of the larger cross-sectional area on the drift speed.
perOption.D: Scales by the current alone, treating the two cross-sectional areas as equal.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A sinusoidal alternating supply of peak voltage 100 V is connected to a diode and a 100 Ω resistor in series.

The diode is ideal with a zero forward resistance and an infinite reverse resistance.

What is the value of the mean current in the resistor?
questions.stemText: A sinusoidal alternating supply of peak voltage 100 V is connected to a diode and a 100 Ω resistor in series. The diode is ideal with a zero forward resistance and an infinite reverse resistance. What is the value of the mean current in the resistor? A less than 0.5 A B 0.5 A C 0.7 A D 1 A

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires comparing a half-wave rectified sine with a half-duty rectangular pulse.
questions.misconception: Halving the peak to get the mean of a half-wave rectified sine.

explanation.body: The diode passes only one half-cycle, and the peak current is $100\ \mathrm{V}/(100\ \Omega)=1.0\ \mathrm{A}$. A current of $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ for half a period and zero for the other half would average $0.5\ \mathrm{A}$. The rectified sinusoid stays below $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ except at its peak, so its mean is less than $0.5\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The conducting half-wave averages less than its peak.
perOption.B: Treats the current as being at its peak throughout the conducting half-cycle.
perOption.C: Uses the approximate r.m.s. current of the unrectified sine wave as the mean.
perOption.D: Uses the peak current as the mean.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A resistor has resistance $R$. When the potential difference across the resistor is $V$, the current in the resistor is $I$. The power dissipated in the resistor is $P$. Work $W$ is done when charge $Q$ flows through the resistor.

What is not a valid relationship between these variables?

A $I=\frac{PQ}{W}$
B $Q=\frac{W}{IR}$
C $R=\frac{V^2}{P}$
D $R=\frac{W}{PQ}$

stemImage.alt: Question 19: A resistor has resistance R. When the potential difference across the resistor is V, the current in the resistor is I. The power dissipated in the resistor is P

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: It requires rearranging the definitions of potential difference, current and power.
questions.misconception: Confusing the reciprocal of current with resistance.

explanation.body: By definition, $V=W/Q=(W/t)/(Q/t)=P/I$. Using $R=V/I$ gives $P=IV=I^2R=V^2/R=W^2/(Q^2R)$. Hence $R=W^2/(PQ^2)$, so D is the invalid relationship.

perOption.A: This relationship is valid because $I=P/V=PQ/W$.
perOption.B: This relationship is valid because $Q=W/V=W/(IR)$.
perOption.C: This relationship is valid because $P=V^2/R$.
perOption.D: Correct. $W/(PQ)=1/I$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: The graph shows the variation with time of a periodic current. What is the root-mean-square value of the current?
questions.stemText: The graph shows the variation with time of a periodic current. What is the root-mean-square value of the current? current 2Io time 1 0 2 3 4 5 -Io A 2 $_{\mathrm{o}}$I B $_{\mathrm{o}}$I 2 C $_{\mathrm{o}}$I 2 D 2 $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{o}}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: It requires reading the time at each level and weighting the squared currents over a period.
questions.misconception: Using the sinusoidal RMS formula for a non-sinusoidal waveform.

explanation.body: In one period, the current is $-I_0$ for two time units and $2I_0$ for one time unit. Squaring, averaging over the period and taking the square root gives $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_0^2+(2I_0)^2}{3}}=\sqrt{2}\,I_0$.

perOption.A: Correct. It is the square root of the time-weighted mean square.
perOption.B: Applies the sinusoidal formula to the lower current magnitude.
perOption.C: Underestimates the mean square by failing to account for the interval at twice the current magnitude.
perOption.D: Uses the peak current in place of the root-mean-square current.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A milliammeter shows a reading of 20 mA. How many electrons flow through the milliammeter in 5.0 s?
questions.stemText: A milliammeter shows a reading of 20 mA. How many electrons flow through the milliammeter in 5.0 s? A 0.10 B 200 C 6.3 x $10^{17}$ D 1.6 x $10^{20}$

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: One-step use of $Q = It$ and $N = Q/e$.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to convert mA or to divide by the electron charge

explanation.body: The total charge is $Q=It=(20\times10^{-3})(5.0)=0.10\ \mathrm{C}$. Dividing by the magnitude of the electron charge gives $N=0.10/(1.6\times10^{-19})=6.3\times10^{17}$.

perOption.A: Gives the transferred charge in coulombs before dividing by the elementary charge.
perOption.B: Fails to convert the current-time product into an electron count using the elementary charge.
perOption.C: Correct. Divide the transferred charge by the charge magnitude per electron.
perOption.D: This many electrons would carry far more than the transferred $0.10\ \mathrm{C}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An alternating current with a rectangular waveform as shown below flows through an $11\ \Omega$ resistor. [Graph: $I$/A against $t$/s. $I = 4.0$ A from 0 to 1 s, $-2.0$ A from 1 to 3 s, 0 from 3 to 4 s; then repeats: 4.0 A from 4 to 5 s, $-2.0$ A from 5 to 7 s, 0 from 7 to 8 s, 4.0 A from 8 to 9 s, $-2.0$ A from 9 s.] What is the average power dissipated by the resistor? A 0 B 44 W C 66 W D 88 W

stemImage.alt: Question 26: An alternating current with a rectangular waveform as shown below flows through an 11  resistor. What is the average power dissipated by the resistor?

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must read the full 4 s period (including the zero interval) and average $I^2R$ rather than $I$.
questions.misconception: Averaging the current (which gives zero net charge) instead of the power, or missing the zero-current interval

explanation.body: Over one period, $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{(4^2\times1+2^2\times2+0\times1)/4}=2.45\ \mathrm{A}$. The average power is $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R=2.45^2\times11=66\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Uses the zero mean current, although power depends on the mean squared current.
perOption.B: Uses the 2 A level alone and ignores the other parts of the waveform.
perOption.C: Correct. The period average of $I^2R$ is 66 W.
perOption.D: Counts the 4 A pulse but omits the power from the negative-current interval.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A wedge-shaped metal conductor of length $L$, varying width and uniform thickness is connected to a cell, as shown.

[The conductor widens linearly from X on the left to Y on the right. Its length is $L$. It is connected in a single loop to a cell with the positive terminal on the X side.]

Which graph best shows how the average drift velocity $v$ of electrons in the conductor varies with distance $x$ from end X?

[All four graphs plot $v$ against $x$ from 0 to $L$. A curves down from a positive value, flattening and staying above zero. B curves up from a positive value and flattens. C is a straight line dropping from a positive value to zero at $L$. D is a straight line increasing from zero at $x=0$.]

appearances.originalFile: grail:10439 CJC.H2.PRELIM.2023.P1.QP
grail:10429 EJC 2023 J2 H2 PRELIM P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer the curve from constant current and linearly increasing cross-sectional area.
questions.misconception: Assuming drift speed falls linearly with area

explanation.body: From $I=nAv_dq$, the drift speed is $v_d=I/(nAq)$. The cross-sectional area increases from X to Y and the current stays constant, so the drift speed decreases. Graphs B and D show an increase, while graph C would mean the electrons stop at Y.

perOption.A: Correct. The drift speed decreases and stays positive at Y.
perOption.B: Shows an increase in drift speed as the cross-sectional area increases.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The variation with time $t$ of the voltage $V$ of an alternating source applied across a $2.5\ \Omega$ resistor is shown below.

[Step graph of $V$ in volts against $t$ in milliseconds from 0 to 10.0. The voltage is 0 from 0 to 1.0 ms, $+4.0\ \mathrm{V}$ from 1.0 to 2.0 ms, and $-1.0\ \mathrm{V}$ from 2.0 to 5.0 ms. This pattern repeats from 5.0 to 10.0 ms.]

What is the mean power dissipated in the resistor?

A $0.98\ \mathrm{W}$; B $1.5\ \mathrm{W}$; C $1.9\ \mathrm{W}$; D $2.4\ \mathrm{W}$

stemImage.alt: Question 27: The variation with time t of the voltage V of an alternating source applied across a 2.5 Ω resistor is shown below. V / V 4.0 t / ms 0 5.0 2.0 3.0 4.0 7.0 10.0

appearances.originalFile: grail:10439 CJC.H2.PRELIM.2023.P1.QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must square each voltage level, weight it by its duration and convert the mean square to power.
questions.misconception: Using mean voltage or a sinusoidal RMS formula for a stepped waveform

explanation.body: Square the voltage and average it over one full $5.0\ \mathrm{ms}$ period, then take the square root. The zero-voltage interval contributes nothing, so $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{(4.0^2\times1.0+(-1.0)^2\times3.0)/5.0}=\sqrt{3.8}\ \mathrm{V}$. The mean power is $V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R=3.8/2.5=1.5\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: $0.98\ \mathrm{W}$ would require a mean-square voltage of $2.45\ \mathrm{V^2}$, but the $4.0\ \mathrm{V}$ pulse alone contributes $3.2\ \mathrm{V^2}$.
perOption.B: Correct. Mean power is mean-square voltage divided by resistance.
perOption.C: Averages only over the four milliseconds with nonzero voltage.
perOption.D: $2.4\ \mathrm{W}$ would require a mean-square voltage of $6.0\ \mathrm{V^2}$, overestimating the contribution of the brief $4.0\ \mathrm{V}$ pulse.

questions.stemText:
A voltage supply connected to a signal generator can either produce an alternating voltage with a sinusoidal waveform or a square waveform with the same peak value of e.m.f. $V_p$ as illustrated below. The voltage supply is connected across a load resistor.

[Two graphs show e.m.f. against time. The sinusoidal waveform completes two cycles between $+V_p$ and $-V_p$, beginning at zero and rising. The square waveform alternates between $+V_p$ and $-V_p$ for equal intervals, beginning at $+V_p$ and completing two cycles.]

What is the ratio of the mean power dissipated in the load resistor by the square waveform to the mean power dissipated in the load resistor by the sinusoidal waveform?

A. 0.25
B. 0.5
C. 2
D. 4

stemImage.alt: Question 27: A voltage supply connected to a signal generator can either produce an alternating voltage with a sinusoidal waveform or a square waveform with the same peak va

appearances.originalFile: grail:14541 CJC 2024.H2.Phy.PRELIM.P1 - QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must read the square wave’s constant voltage magnitude and compare its mean power with that of a sine wave.
questions.misconception: Confusing peak voltage, rms voltage and mean power

explanation.body: The mean power in the resistor is $\langle P\rangle=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R$. The sine wave has $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=V_p/\sqrt{2}$, giving mean power $V_p^2/(2R)$. The square wave has magnitude $V_p$ throughout, so its rms voltage is $V_p$ and its mean power is $V_p^2/R$. The ratio is $2$.

perOption.B: Inverts the requested ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats the sine wave’s rms voltage as half its peak voltage.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two metal wires X and Y are connected in series and a current is flowing through them. The number of free electrons per cubic metre in wire X is twice that in wire Y. The diameter of the wire X is half that of wire Y.

The drift speed of the free electrons in wire X is 0.52 mm $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

What is the drift speed of the free electrons in wire Y?
questions.stemText: Two metal wires X and Y are connected in series and a current is flowing through them. The number of free electrons per cubic metre in wire X is twice that in wire Y. The diameter of the wire X is half that of wire Y. The drift speed of the free electrons in wire X is 0.52 mm s-1. What is the drift speed of the free electrons in wire Y? A 0.26 mm $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 0.52 mm $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 1.04 mm $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 2.08 mm $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Single application of $I = nAvq$ with two ratio changes.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that area scales with diameter squared

explanation.body: For each wire, $I=enAv=en(\pi d^2/4)v$. The wires are in series, so $I_X=I_Y$ and $n_Xd_X^2v_X=n_Yd_Y^2v_Y$. Hence $v_Y=(n_X/n_Y)(d_X/d_Y)^2v_X=2(1/2)^2(0.52)=0.26\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the diameter ratio directly as the area ratio.
perOption.C: Accounts for the density ratio alone and ignores the different areas.
perOption.D: Inverts the area ratio and omits the density ratio.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A sinusoidal alternating current of root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value I is passed through a resistor of resistance 2.0 Ω.

Which graph shows how the power P dissipated in the resistor varies with time t?
questions.stemText: A sinusoidal alternating current of root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value I is passed through a resistor of resistance 2.0 Ω. Which graph shows how the power P dissipated in the resistor varies with time t? A P $ξ2I^{2}$ t B P $ξ2I^{2}$ t C P $2I^{2}$ t D P $4I^{2}$ t

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combines r.m.s.-to-peak conversion with the $\sin^2$ shape of power.
questions.misconception: Using the r.m.s. current as the peak, or a $|\sin|$ shape for power

explanation.body: The instantaneous power is $P=I_0^2R\sin^2(\omega t)$, so the graph has smooth minima at zero. The mean power is $\langle P\rangle=I^2R$. The peak is twice the mean, giving $P_0=2I^2R=2I^2(2)=4I^2$.

perOption.A: The sharp minima resemble a rectified sine rather than a squared sine.
perOption.B: The curve has the right shape but peaks at $\sqrt{2}I^2$ instead of $4I^2$.

C. $\frac{3V_0^2}{\sqrt{2}\,R}$

questions.difficultyReason: The diode changes the equivalent resistance between half-cycles, so the two power averages must be combined.

explanation.body: When the diode is forward-biased, the equivalent resistance is $R/2$, so the peak power is $V_0^2/(R/2)$ and the half-cycle mean is $V_0^2/R$. Which of the following statements is incorrect?

A The resistance of the resistor is $3\ \Omega$.
B The energy dissipated in the resistor is $12\ \mathrm{J}$.
C The charge passing through the resistor is $20\ \mathrm{C}$.
D The potential difference across the resistor is $6\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$.

questions.difficultyReason: Uses direct substitutions and the definition of a volt to identify the incorrect statement.
questions.misconception: Confusing power with energy

explanation.body: The energy dissipated is $E=IVt=(2)(6)(10)=120\ \mathrm{J}$. The statement giving $12\ \mathrm{J}$ is therefore incorrect.

perOption.A: The statement is true because $R=V/I=3\ \Omega$.
perOption.B: Correct. The value 12 is the power in watts.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A heater is connected to a $110\ \mathrm{V}$ sinusoidal alternating current and it dissipates energy at a mean rate of $800\ \mathrm{W}$. The same heater, with its resistance unchanged, is then connected to a $156\ \mathrm{V}$ d.c. supply. At what rate does the heater dissipate energy now?

A $400\ \mathrm{W}$
B $800\ \mathrm{W}$
C $1100\ \mathrm{W}$
D $1600\ \mathrm{W}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:16192 2018 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Uses the r.m.s. supply voltage to find resistance and applies the same power equation to the d.c. supply.
questions.misconception: Assuming equal peak voltages give equal average heating

explanation.body: Using the a.c. voltage as an r.m.s. value, the heater resistance is $R=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/P=110^2/800=15.125\ \Omega$. On the d.c. supply the power is $P=V_{\mathrm{DC}}^2/R=156^2/15.125=1609\ \mathrm{W}$, which rounds to $1600\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Halves the original mean power even though the effective voltage increases.
perOption.B: Treats the d.c. voltage as equivalent to the original a.c. r.m.s. voltage.
perOption.C: Scales the power linearly with voltage instead of using the squared voltage ratio.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.misconception: Leaving out the zero-current interval

explanation.body: Over one period, the current takes the values $4$, $8$, $-5$ and $0\ \mathrm A$ for equal intervals. The root-mean-square current is $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{(4^2+8^2+5^2+0^2)/4}=5.12\ \mathrm A$.

perOption.A: Averages the current magnitudes without squaring them before taking the square root.
perOption.B: Correct. All four intervals count toward the mean.

perOption.D: Gives the mean square and omits the square root.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Transmission cables of total resistance $R$ are used to transfer electrical energy from an a.c. generator in a power station to a factory located several kilometers away.

The power and voltage outputs of the generator are $P$ and $V$ respectively. The potential difference across the transmission cables is $V_{\mathrm c}$.

What is the power input to the factory?

A. $P+\left(\frac P V\right)^2R$
B. $P+\left(\frac P {V_{\mathrm c}}\right)^2R$
C. $P-\left(\frac P V\right)^2R$
D. $P-\left(\frac P {V_{\mathrm c}}\right)^2R$

stemImage.alt: Question 28: Transmission cables of total resistance R are used to transfer electrical energy from an a.c. generator in a power station to a factory located several kilomete

appearances.originalFile: grail:16202 2020 RI Prelims H2 Phy Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: It requires finding the line current and subtracting cable losses.
questions.misconception: Using the cable voltage drop with the total generator power.

explanation.body: The factory input is the generator output less the cable loss, so $P_{\mathrm{factory}}=P-I^2R$. Substituting $I=P/V$ gives $P_{\mathrm{factory}}=P-(P/V)^2R$.

perOption.A: Adds the cable loss to the power delivered.
perOption.B: Adds the cable loss and incorrectly uses the cable drop to find the current from total power.
perOption.C: Correct. It subtracts the cable’s resistive loss.
perOption.D: Uses the cable drop with the whole generator power to calculate the current.

During this process, 2500 J of energy is dissipated in the resistor R and 500 J is dissipated in the battery. What is the e.m.f. of the battery? A 0.50 V B 0.33 V C 1.7 V D 2.0 V

questions.difficultyReason: The student adds the two energy losses and divides by the charge.
questions.misconception: Equating e.m.f. with terminal potential difference

explanation.body: The battery supplies $2500+500=3000\ \mathrm J$ in total, including the energy dissipated inside it. Its e.m.f. is the total energy supplied per unit charge, so $\mathcal E=3000/1500=2.00\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: This would account for only 750 J of the 3000 J supplied.
perOption.B: Divides only the energy lost inside the battery by the charge.
perOption.C: Divides only the energy dissipated in the external resistor by the charge.
perOption.D: Correct. It includes both energy losses per unit charge.

B $\sqrt{2}P$

questions.misconception: Assuming mean power scales linearly with peak current or frequency

explanation.body: The original mean power is $P=I_0^2R/2$. After doubling the peak current, $P'=(2I_0)^2R/2=4P$. Halving the frequency changes the period and leaves the mean over a cycle unchanged.

perOption.A: Treats the changes as cancelling, although frequency does not enter the mean power.
perOption.B: Misapplies the $\sqrt{2}$ peak-to-r.m.s. factor to the power ratio, even though it is the same for both currents.

explanation.body: The current through the specimen is the same at every section, so $I_X=I_Y=I_Z$. Since $I=nevA$ and $I$, $n$ and $e$ are constant, drift speed varies inversely with cross-sectional area. X is narrowest and Y widest, giving $v_X>v_Z>v_Y$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A metal wire of length $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ and uniform cross-sectional area contains $4.8\times10^{22}$ free electrons. When a potential difference is applied across the ends of the wire, the free electrons move with an average drift speed of $3.2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

A $0.0098\ \mathrm{A}$
B $0.050\ \mathrm{A}$
C $1.2\ \mathrm{A}$

questions.difficultyReason: Convert the total electron count into a number per unit length before applying the drift-current equation.
questions.misconception: Using the total carrier count as a number density.

explanation.body: Use $I=nAve$, with $n=N_e/(AL)$ for $N_e$ free electrons in the wire. The area cancels, giving $I=(N_e/L)ve$. Substitution yields $I=(4.8\times10^{22}/0.20)(3.2\times10^{-5})(1.60\times10^{-19})=1.2\ \mathrm A$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the number of carriers per metre, giving a current two orders of magnitude too small.

The middle branch runs from the left rail through $R_4$, left-facing diode $\mathrm{D}_2$ and $R_3$ to the right rail. Resistor $R_2$ connects the junction of $\mathrm{D}_1$ and $R_1$ to the junction of $\mathrm{D}_2$ and $R_3$.]

A. $0.25V_0^2/R$
B. $0.36V_0^2/R$
C. $0.39V_0^2/R$
D. $0.79V_0^2/R$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: In the circuit shown, D1 and D2 are ideal diodes. Resistor R1 has a resistance of 2R. Resistors R2, R3 and R4 are identical and have the same resistance R. The

appearances.originalFile: grail:19905 2025 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 Questions

questions.difficultyReason: It requires reducing two different resistor networks and averaging their sinusoidal power over a full cycle.
questions.misconception: Using one equivalent resistance for the entire cycle.

explanation.body: In the first half-cycle, only $\mathrm{D}_1$ conducts and the effective resistance is $R$. In the second half-cycle, only $\mathrm{D}_2$ conducts and the effective resistance is $1.75R$. questions.stemText:
A cylindrical copper wire of radius $r$, length $L$ and resistivity $\rho$ is connected across a constant voltage source of e.m.f. $E$ with negligible internal resistance. The wire contains $n$ free electrons per unit volume, each carrying a charge $e$.

Which of the following expressions correctly represents the drift velocity of the electrons in the wire?

A. $\frac{E}{ne\rho L}$
B. $\frac{E(\pi r^2)}{ne\rho L^3}$
C. $\frac{EL}{ne\rho(\pi r^2)^2}$
D. $\frac{E}{ne\rho L(\pi r^2)}$

stemImage.alt: Question 22: A cylindrical copper wire of radius r, length L and resistivity  is connected across a constant voltage source of e.m.f. E with negligible internal resistance.

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combines the current and resistance equations and cancels area.
questions.misconception: Assuming radius affects drift speed at fixed voltage

explanation.body: Using $V=IR$, substitute $I=nAve$ and $R=\rho L/A$ to get $E=(nAve)(\rho L/A)=nve\rho L$. Therefore $v=E/(ne\rho L)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Retains a spurious area factor and assigns the wrong power to length.
perOption.C: Introduces an inverse-square area dependence and puts length in the numerator.
perOption.D: Retains an extra area factor in the denominator.

questions.stemText:
A beam of beta particles constitutes a current of $10.0\ \mathrm{\mu A}$. Given that these beta particles travel at a speed of $2.5\times10^7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, what is the average number of beta particles found in one centimetre length of this beam?

A $2.5\times10^4$
B $4.0\times10^4$
C $2.5\times10^6$
D $4.0\times10^6$

stemImage.alt: Question 21: A beam of beta particles constitutes a current of 10.0 µA. Given that these beta particles travel at a speed of 2.5 × 107 m s−1, what is the average number of b

appearances.originalFile: grail:10493 RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Convert current to a particle rate and divide by the distance travelled per second in centimetres.
questions.misconception: Using metres when the question asks for particles per centimetre

explanation.body: Using $I=Ne/t$, the number of particles passing per second is $I/e=(10.0\times10^{-6})/(1.6\times10^{-19})=6.25\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. In one second the particles travel $2.5\times10^7\ \mathrm{m}=2.5\times10^9\ \mathrm{cm}$, so one centimetre contains $(6.25\times10^{13})/(2.5\times10^9)=25\,000$ particles on average.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Overcounts the particles per centimetre, as can happen if the elementary charge is rounded down to $1.0\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$.
perOption.C: Gives the number in one metre of beam.

When a steady direct current of value $I$ passes through a heating element of resistance $R$, the time taken to raise the temperature of water of mass $m$ by $10\ \mathrm{K}$ is $T$.

When a sinusoidal alternating current with a peak current of value $I$ passes through a heating element of resistance $2R$, what is the time taken to raise water of mass $m$ by $10\ \mathrm{K}$?

A $\sqrt{2}\,T$
B $T$
C $T/2$
D $T/4$

questions.difficultyReason: The student must square the r.m.s. current and compare the heating times at the same energy transfer.
questions.misconception: Using peak current to calculate mean power.

explanation.body: The heating time is $t=mc\Delta\theta/P$. For steady d.c., $P=I^2R$, so $T=mc\Delta\theta/(I^2R)$. For a.c., the mean power is $(I/\sqrt{2})^2(2R)=I^2R$, so the heating time is also $T$.

A sinusoidal current of peak value $I_o$ is passed through a resistor $R$ with a diode connected in series with it. The average rate of heat dissipated in $R$ is

A $0.25I_o^2R$
B $0.50I_o^2R$
C $0.71I_o^2R$
D $1.0I_o^2R$

stemImage.alt: Question 28: A sinusoidal current of peak value Io is passed through a resistor R with a diode connected in series with it. The average rate of heat dissipated in R is

appearances.originalFile: grail:19907 RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Students combine sinusoidal mean power with the effect of half-wave rectification.
questions.misconception: Averaging power only over the conducting half-cycle

explanation.body: Without the diode, the average power is $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R=0.50I_o^2R$. The diode allows power to be dissipated during only one of the two equal-power half-cycles, so the full-cycle average is halved to $0.25I_o^2R$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the average power of the unrectified sine wave.

questions.stemText:
A half wave rectified sinusoidal and a square wave current are passed separately through the same resistor. In each case, the resistor dissipates the same mean power.

[Two graphs of current against time, each with the origin marked 0 and one period marked $T$. The half wave rectified sinusoidal wave has a positive sinusoidal half-cycle followed by zero current for half a cycle, and repeats at $T$. The square wave alternates between equal positive and negative current magnitudes, each for half a cycle, and repeats at $T$.]

What is the ratio $\frac{\text{peak current of square wave}}{\text{peak current of half wave rectified sinusoidal wave}}$?

A  $\frac12$
B  $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
C  $1$
D  $2$

stemImage.alt: Question 21: A half wave rectified sinusoidal and a square wave current are passed separately through the same resistor. In each case, the resistor dissipates the same mean

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Compare the mean squares of two waveforms over a full cycle before equating the powers.
questions.misconception: Using the full sine-wave RMS factor for a half-wave rectified sine

explanation.body: For the half-wave rectified sine, the mean of the squared current during the conducting half-cycle is $I_0^2/2$, so over the full cycle it is $I_0^2/4$. Taking the square root gives an RMS current of $I_0/2$. The square wave has constant current magnitude, so its RMS current equals its peak current. Equal mean powers in the same resistor give equal RMS currents, hence the requested peak-current ratio is $1/2$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This uses the RMS factor for a full sinusoidal wave and overlooks the zero-current half-cycle.
perOption.C: This equates peak currents even though equal mean power fixes the RMS currents.
perOption.D: This inverts the requested peak-current ratio.

[The graph plots $P/\mathrm{W}$ against $t/\mathrm{s}$. Three identical peaks reach $150\ \mathrm{W}$, and the power is zero at $0$, $0.010$, $0.020$ and $0.030\ \mathrm{s}$.]

Which equation represents the sinusoidal alternating current through the resistor?

A $I=5.0\sin(100\pi t)$
B $I=5.0\sin(200\pi t)$
C $I=25\sin(100\pi t)$
D $I=25\sin(300\pi t)$

questions.difficultyReason: It requires extracting the peak power and recognising that current takes two power cycles to repeat.
questions.misconception: Equating the periods of power and current

explanation.body: The peak current is $I_0=\sqrt{P_0/R}=\sqrt{150/6.0}=5.0\ \mathrm{A}$. Because $P=I^2R$, the current period is twice the power period, so $T=0.020\ \mathrm{s}$. Substituting gives $I=I_0\sin(2\pi t/T)=5.0\sin(100\pi t)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the power period as the current period.
perOption.C: Uses the peak value of current squared as the peak current.
perOption.D: Uses 25 A as the amplitude and an angular frequency that does not match the zero crossings.

In the circuit shown, lamp P is rated 250 V, 50 W and lamp Q is rated 250 V, 200 W. The two lamps are connected in series to a 250 V power supply.

Assume that the resistance of each lamp remains constant.

Which statement most accurately describes what happens when the switch is closed?
questions.stemText: In the circuit shown, lamp P is rated 250 V, 50 W and lamp Q is rated 250 V, 200 W. The two lamps are connected in series to a 250 V power supply. Assume that the resistance of each lamp remains constant. Which statement most accurately describes what happens when the switch is closed? A Lamp P emits four times as much power as lamp Q. B Lamp P emits twice as much power as lamp Q. C Lamp Q emits four times as much power as lamp P. D Lamp Q emits twice as much power as lamp P.

options.label: A
options.text: Lamp P emits four times as much power as lamp Q.

options.label: B
options.text: Lamp P emits twice as much power as lamp Q.

options.label: C
options.text: Lamp Q emits four times as much power as lamp P.

options.label: D
options.text: Lamp Q emits twice as much power as lamp P.

appearances.originalFile: grail:10478 SAJC Prelim (H2) P1 2023

questions.difficultyReason: Requires applying power equations under two different operating conditions.
questions.misconception: Using the nameplate power as the series power.

explanation.body: At the same rated voltage $V$, Q has four times the power of P, so $V^2/R_Q=4V^2/R_P$ and $R_P=4R_Q$. The lamps carry the same current in series. Therefore $P'_P=I^2R_P=4I^2R_Q=4P'_Q$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Underestimates the resistance ratio and hence the power ratio.
perOption.C: Uses the rated powers as though the lamps still had equal voltages.
perOption.D: Reverses which lamp has the greater resistance and understates the ratio.

What is the mean power dissipated in the load resistor at the higher frequency? A 200 W B 400 W C 800 W D 1600 W

appearances.originalFile: grail:10478 SAJC Prelim (H2) P1 2023

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognition that mean power depends on RMS current at fixed amplitude.
questions.misconception: Using peak current to calculate mean power.

explanation.body: At fixed peak current, changing the frequency does not change the mean power in the resistor. The mean power is $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R=(2.0/\sqrt2)^2(200)=400\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Halves the mean power when the frequency doubles.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Substitutes the peak current and obtains the peak power.
perOption.D: Doubles the peak power because the frequency doubles.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14594 (SAJC) 2024 H2 Phy Prelim P1_qn and soln_for sharing

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recalling the definition of potential difference.
questions.misconception: Confusing energy per charge with force per charge.

explanation.body: The potential difference is the electrical work done per unit charge, $V=W/Q$. It measures the energy transferred for each coulomb passing through the component.

perOption.A: Charge per unit time is current.
perOption.B: Correct. Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge.
perOption.C: Force per unit positive charge is electric field strength.
perOption.D: For a resistive component, multiplying resistance by current gives the potential difference.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must equate resistor powers and then convert the rms current to its peak value.
questions.misconception: Confusing the rms current with the peak current

explanation.body: Equal power gives $I^2R=I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2(R/4)$, so $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=2I$. For a sinusoid the peak current is $I_0=\sqrt{2}\,I_{\mathrm{rms}}=2\sqrt{2}\,I$.

perOption.A: This makes the peak conversion but ignores the reduction in resistance.
perOption.B: $2I$ is the rms value, so it still needs the peak conversion.

questions.stem:
In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, the electron moves in a circular orbit of radius 5.3 x $10^{-11}$ m about the nucleus with a uniform angular speed of 4.1 x $10^{16}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

What is the average current at a point on the electron orbit?
questions.stemText: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, the electron moves in a circular orbit of radius 5.3 x 10-11 m about the nucleus with a uniform angular speed of 4.1 x 1016 rad s-1. What is the average current at a point on the electron orbit? A 2.5 x $10^{-35}$ A B 1.6 x $10^{-19}$ A C 3.5 x $10^{-13}$ A D 1.0 x $10^{-3}$ A

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the period from angular speed and counting the charge that passes in one revolution.
questions.misconception: Using orbital speed instead of revolution frequency

explanation.body: In one period, one elementary charge passes a given point on the orbit. With $\omega=4.1\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, the period is $T=2\pi/\omega$. The average current is $I=e/T=(1.60\times10^{-19})/(2\pi/\omega)\approx1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies charge by the period instead of dividing by it.
perOption.B: Gives the elementary charge without accounting for how often it passes the point.
perOption.C: Multiplies charge by orbital speed instead of revolutions per second.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A variable resistor dissipates a certain power when a steady current I flows through it. The resistance had to be halved to obtain the same power dissipation in the resistor when a sinusoidal alternating current is used with a diode in series with the resistor in the circuit. What is the peak value of the alternating current?
questions.stemText: A variable resistor dissipates a certain power when a steady current I flows through it. The resistance had to be halved to obtain the same power dissipation in the resistor when a sinusoidal alternating current is used with a diode in series with the resistor in the circuit. What is the peak value of the alternating current? A I B 1.4 I C 2 I D 2.8 I

appearances.originalFile: grail:9660 TJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the half-wave rectified rms current and the halved resistance combined.
questions.misconception: Uses the full-wave $I_0/\sqrt2$ rms for a half-wave signal.

explanation.body:
For the steady current, $P = I^2R$.

For half-wave rectified a.c. the rms current is $I_0/2$, and the resistance is now $\tfrac12 R$:

$P = \left(\dfrac{I_0}{2}\right)^2\left(\dfrac12 R\right) = I^2R$

So $I_0 = \sqrt{8}\,I = 2.8\,I$.

perOption.A: Ignores the halving of resistance and the half-wave factor.
perOption.B: Uses $I_0=\sqrt2 I$, the full-wave result, and ignores the diode and halved resistance.
perOption.C: Ignores the factor from the halved resistance.
perOption.D: Correct. $I_0=\sqrt{8}\,I = 2.8\,I$.

questions.stem: A 240 V electric heater uses a current of 2.0 A. It is to be rewound with resistance wire of diameter 6.0 × $10^{-4}$ m. At working temperature, the resistance wire has resistivity of 1.4 $\times 10^{-6}$ Ω m. What length of wire is required?
questions.stemText: A 240 V electric heater uses a current of 2.0 A. It is to be rewound with resistance wire of diameter 6.0 × 10–4 m. At working temperature, the resistance wire has resistivity of 1.4 ×10–6 Ω m. What length of wire is required? A 6.0 m B 24 m C 51 m D 97 m

appearances.originalFile: grail:10482 TJC 2023 H2 Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Combine Ohm's law with the resistivity formula; common slip is using diameter for radius.
questions.misconception: Using diameter instead of radius in the area

explanation.body:
$R = \rho L/A$ and $R = V/I$, so $V/I = \rho L/A$ and $L = VA/(I\rho)$.

$L = \dfrac{240\,[\pi(3.0\times10^{-4})^2]}{2.0 \times 1.4\times10^{-6}} = 24\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Too small; check the area $A=\pi r^2$ and the factor of $I\rho$ in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct. $L = VA/(I\rho) = 24$ m.
perOption.C: Not from the school's working; likely an arithmetic slip in the area.
perOption.D: About four times the answer, from using the diameter as the radius in $A = \pi r^2$.

The secondary coil is connected to a lamp of resistance 6.0 . The transformer is 100% efficient. What is the peak power dissipated by the lamp? A 12 W B 24 W C 48 W D 96 W

questions.difficultyReason: Chains transformer turns ratio, r.m.s. to peak conversion and power, with the peak-versus-mean trap.
questions.misconception: Using r.m.s. values to get the mean power but reporting it as the peak power.

explanation.body:
$\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} \Rightarrow V_s = \dfrac{130}{2500} \times 230 = 12\ \mathrm{V}$ (r.m.s.).

Peak power $= \dfrac{V_0^2}{R} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{2} \times 12)^2}{6} = 48\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: 12 is the r.m.s. secondary voltage, not a power.
perOption.B: This is the mean power $V_{rms}^2/R = 24$ W, not the peak power.

Given that the drift velocity of electrons in the rod is 2.3 × $10^{-5}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, what is the resistance of the rod?
questions.stemText: A uniform copper rod of cross-sectional area 8.0 mm2 has 8.2 × 1028 conduction electrons per cubic metre. A current flows through the rod when a potential difference of 3.0 V is applied across it. Given that the drift velocity of electrons in the rod is 2.3 × 10−5 m s−1, what is the resistance of the rod? A 0.08 Ω B 0.16 Ω C 0.80 Ω D 1.2 Ω

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert the area and use the drift-current and resistance equations in sequence.
questions.misconception: Square millimetres convert to square metres by a factor of $10^{-3}$.

explanation.body: The drift current is $I=nqvA=(8.2\times10^{28})(1.6\times10^{-19})(2.3\times10^{-5})(8.0\times10^{-6})=2.41\ \mathrm{A}$. The resistance is $R=V/I=3.0/2.41=1.2\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Would require a current of about $38\ \mathrm{A}$, much larger than the drift current.
perOption.B: Would require a current of about $19\ \mathrm{A}$, much larger than the drift current.
perOption.C: Implies a current of $3.75\ \mathrm{A}$, overestimating the drift current.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stem:
The figure below shows the variation with time, t, of a periodic voltage supply, V.

What is the root-mean-square value of the voltage?
questions.stemText: The figure below shows the variation with time, t, of a periodic voltage supply, V. V / V t / ms What is the root-mean-square value of the voltage? A 12 V B 23 V C 33 V D 529 V

appearances.originalFile: grail:10511 TMJC_2023_H2 Physics_P1_QP

questions.difficultyReason: Requires applying the r.m.s. definition to a non-sinusoidal pulse waveform read from a graph.
questions.misconception: applying $V_0/\sqrt{2}$ to a non-sinusoidal waveform

explanation.body:
Consider one period ($1.0\ \mathrm{ms}$), in which $V = 46\ \mathrm{V}$ for $0.25\ \mathrm{ms}$ and zero otherwise.

1. Square the graph: $V^2 = 46^2 = 2116\ \mathrm{V^2}$.

2. Mean over one period: $\langle V^2 \rangle = \dfrac{\text{area}}{\text{period}} = \dfrac{(2116)(0.25\times10^{-3})}{1.0\times10^{-3}} = 529\ \mathrm{V^2}$.

3. Take the square root: $V_{rms} = \sqrt{529} = 23\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: This is roughly the mean voltage ($46 \times 0.25 \approx 12\ \mathrm{V}$), not the r.m.s. value.
perOption.B: Correct. $\sqrt{\langle V^2\rangle} = \sqrt{529} = 23\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.C: Uses $V_0/\sqrt{2}$, which applies only to sinusoidal voltages.
perOption.D: Gives the mean of $V^2$ but forgets to take the square root.

When another sinusoidal alternating current passes through the same resistor of resistance R, the mean power dissipated in the resistor is 4P. What is the root-mean-square value of this current? A I 0 2 B $_{0}$I C 2I 0 D 2I 0

appearances.originalFile: grail:15121 TMJC_2024_H2 Physics P1_QP_AS

questions.difficultyReason: Combines the peak-to-r.m.s. conversion with the square-law dependence of power on current.
questions.misconception: Treating peak current as r.m.s. current

explanation.body: The second mean power is $P'=4P=4(I_0/\sqrt{2})^2R$. Since $P'=(I'_{\mathrm{rms}})^2R$, cancelling $R$ gives $(I'_{\mathrm{rms}})^2=2I_0^2$. Taking the square root gives $I'_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{2}I_0$.

perOption.A: This is the r.m.s. current of the original sinusoid.
perOption.B: An r.m.s. current of $I_0$ would dissipate only $2P$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Doubles the original peak current and reports it as the new r.m.s. current.

appearances.originalFile: grail:19911 TMJC_2025_H2 Physics_P1_QP

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding r.m.s. values for sinusoidal, rectified and square waveforms.
questions.misconception: Treating every waveform's peak as if it were its r.m.s. value

explanation.body:
Mean power is $V_{\text{rms}}^2/R$ for each waveform:

A (sinusoid): $\dfrac{(60/\sqrt{2})^2}{8.0} = 225\ \mathrm{W}$

B (half-wave sinusoid): $\tfrac{1}{2}(225) = 112.5\ \mathrm{W}$

C (square wave): $\dfrac{60^2}{8.0} = 450\ \mathrm{W}$

D (square wave, on half the time): $\tfrac{1}{2}(450) = 225\ \mathrm{W}$

Only C gives $450\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: A sinusoid of peak 60 V has $V_{\text{rms}} = 60/\sqrt{2}$, giving only 225 W.
perOption.B: The half-wave sinusoid gives half of 225 W, i.e. 112.5 W.
perOption.C: Correct. A ±60 V square wave has $V_{\text{rms}} = 60\ \mathrm{V}$, so $P = 60^2/8.0 = 450\ \mathrm{W}$.
perOption.D: The voltage is zero for half of each cycle, so the mean power is half of 450 W, i.e. 225 W.

appearances.originalFile: grail:19911 TMJC_2025_H2 Physics_P1_QP

questions.difficultyReason: Students must trace current paths through a diode bridge for both half-cycles, which is less familiar than single-diode rectification.
questions.misconception: Thinking a diode circuit always gives half-wave output

explanation.body:
Current from the a.c. supply flows in both directions around the circuit as the supply alternates.

However, the arrangement of the four diodes (a bridge) makes the current through R flow only upward in both half-cycles. So both halves of each cycle appear across R with the same polarity: a full-wave rectified trace.

perOption.A: Shows the unrectified a.c.; the diodes stop the current through R from ever reversing.
perOption.B: Correct. Both half-cycles pass through R in the same direction (full-wave rectification).
perOption.C: This is half-wave rectification from a single diode; the bridge conducts during both half-cycles.
perOption.D: Assumes the diodes block all current; in each half-cycle one pair of diodes conducts through R.

questions.stem:
A high potential difference is applied between the electrodes of a mercury (Hg) discharge tube such that the gas between the electrodes is ionized.

In each minute, 1.5 × $10^{15}$ electrons and 4.4 × $10^{15}$ positive mercury ions (singly charged) move past a cross-section of the tube in opposite directions.

What is the total current between the electrodes?
questions.stemText: A high potential difference is applied between the electrodes of a mercury (Hg) discharge tube such that the gas between the electrodes is ionized. − + positive negative + − electrode electrode + Hg+ In each minute, 1.5 × 1015 electrons and 4.4 × 1015 positive mercury ions (singly charged) move past a cross-section of the tube in opposite directions. What is the total current between the electrodes? A 8.0 µA B 16 µA C 0.46 mA D 0.94 mA

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine the two charge flows and convert a per-minute count into current.
questions.misconception: Subtracting currents for opposite charge motions

explanation.body: The electrons and positive mercury ions move in opposite directions, so their conventional currents add. In one minute the effective charge transferred is $Q=(1.5\times10^{15}+4.4\times10^{15})(1.6\times10^{-19})=9.44\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm C$. Thus $I=Q/t=(9.44\times10^{-4})/60=1.57\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm A\approx16\ \mu\mathrm A$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the charge-carrier counts even though both streams contribute current in the same direction.
perOption.B: Correct.

questions.stem:
Two wires of the same material and length are connected in series in an electrical circuit. One wire is thicker than the other.

Which of the following statements is true when a current flows in the circuit?
questions.stemText: Two wires of the same material and length are connected in series in an electrical circuit. One wire is thicker than the other. Which of the following statements is true when a current flows in the circuit? A The drift speed of electrons in the thicker wire is higher than the thinner wire. B The drift speed of electrons in the thicker wire is lower than the thinner wire. C The number density of charge carriers in the thicker wire is higher than the thinner wire. D The number density of charge carriers in the thicker wire is lower than the thinner wire.

options.label: A
options.text: The drift speed of electrons in the thicker wire is higher than the thinner wire.

options.label: B
options.text: The drift speed of electrons in the thicker wire is lower than the thinner wire.

options.label: C
options.text: The number density of charge carriers in the thicker wire is higher than the thinner wire.

options.label: D
options.text: The number density of charge carriers in the thicker wire is lower than the thinner wire.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14599 (VJC) 2024 H2 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Identify the quantities shared by both wires in the drift-current equation.
questions.misconception: Confusing carrier number density with cross-sectional area.

explanation.body: The series wires carry the same current $I=nAvq$. Their common material gives the same carrier number density $n$, and the electron charge magnitude is $q=e$ in both. The thicker wire has a larger area $A$, so its drift speed $v$ is lower.

perOption.A: Reverses the dependence of drift speed on area at fixed current.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Confuses larger area with higher carrier number density.
perOption.D: Assumes the same material has a lower carrier number density when formed into a thicker wire.

$f/\mathrm{Hz}$, $I_{\mathrm{r.m.s.}}/\mathrm{A}$
A 20, 1.6

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A sinusoidal alternating supply is connected to a 10 Ω resistor in series. The graph shows how the power P dissipated across the resistor varies with time t. P

appearances.originalFile: grail:14599 (VJC) 2024 H2 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The power period and peak current both need converting.
questions.misconception: Confusing the power and current periods

explanation.body:
Four power cycles take $100\ \mathrm{ms}$, which is two current cycles because the power period is half the current period. Thus $T=50\ \mathrm{ms}$ and $f=1/(50\times10^{-3})=20\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

From $P_{\max}=I_0^2R$, the peak current is $I_0=\sqrt{50/10}=2.24\ \mathrm{A}$. Hence $I_{\mathrm{r.m.s.}}=2.24/\sqrt2=1.58\ \mathrm{A}\approx1.6\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.B: Uses the power period as the current period.
perOption.C: Uses the peak current as the r.m.s. current.
perOption.D: Uses the power period and the peak current.

questions.difficultyReason: The mean-power formula gives the frequency dependence directly.

explanation.body: The mean rate of heat production is $P=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R$. Both $V_{\mathrm{rms}}$ and $R$ are fixed, so $P$ is independent of $f$.

perOption.A: Assumes each cycle releases a fixed amount of heat as the number of cycles per second increases.
perOption.B: Introduces a square-root frequency dependence even though both quantities in the power formula are fixed.

questions.stemText:
An electric current of $12\ \mathrm{A}$ flows in a wire of length $0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ and diameter $1.5\ \mathrm{mm}$.

The average drift speed of the free electrons in the wire is $5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

How many free electrons are there in the wire?

A $1.3\times10^{16}$
B $5.3\times10^{22}$
C $1.5\times10^{23}$
D $4.3\times10^{23}$

stemImage.alt: Question 20: An electric current of 12 A flows in a wire of length 0.35 m and diameter 1.5 mm. The average drift speed of the free electrons in the wire is 5.0 x 10−4 m s−1.

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Connect number density to total electron count and recognize that the cross-sectional area cancels.
questions.misconception: Confusing number density with the total number of electrons.

explanation.body: Use $I=nAve$, where $n=N/(AL)$ for a wire with $N$ free electrons and length $L$. Substituting gives $I=Nve/L$. Hence $N=IL/(ve)=(12)(0.35)/[(5.0\times10^{-4})(1.6\times10^{-19})]=5.25\times10^{22}$, or $5.3\times10^{22}$.

perOption.A: Severely undercounts the electrons by retaining an area factor even though the area cancels.
perOption.B: Correct. The wire contains about $5.3\times10^{22}$ free electrons.
perOption.C: Omits the $0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ length factor, giving the number per metre.
perOption.D: Overcounts the electrons by using inconsistent factors for the wire dimensions where the area should cancel.

questions.stemText: The graph below shows how the voltage of an a.c. source V varies with time t. V / V 3.00 0 t / ms 6.00 2.00 3.00 5.00 4.00 1.00 −2.00 What is the r.m.s. voltage of the source? A 2.12 V B 2.38 V C 2.50 V D 2.55 V

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Read the time spent at each voltage and weight the squared levels over one period.
questions.misconception: Giving unequal-duration levels equal weight.

explanation.body: Square the voltage graph to get $9.00\ \mathrm{V^2}$ for $1.00\ \mathrm{ms}$ and $4.00\ \mathrm{V^2}$ for $2.00\ \mathrm{ms}$ in each period. The mean square is $[9.00+2(4.00)]/3=5.6667\ \mathrm{V^2}$. Taking the square root gives an r.m.s. voltage of $2.38\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Applies the sinusoidal peak-to-r.m.s. factor to a rectangular waveform.

questions.stemText: The r.m.s. value of an alternating sinusoidal current in a load resistor is 2.0 A and the mean power dissipated in the resistor of resistance R is the same as that of a steady current I in another resistor of resistance 2R. What is the value of the steady current I? A 0.71 A B 1.4 A C 2.0 A D 4.0 A

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Equates two power expressions, one of which uses the r.m.s. current.
questions.misconception: Treating r.m.s. current as needing a further $\sqrt{2}$ conversion

explanation.body:
Mean power in the a.c. resistor $= I_\mathrm{rms}^2 R = (2.0)^2 R = 4R$.

Mean power with the steady current $= I^2(2R) = 4R$, so $I^2 = 2$ and $I = 1.4\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Introduces an extra factor of $1/2$, for example by treating 2.0 A as a peak value and halving again.
perOption.C: Ignores that the steady current flows through $2R$, not $R$.
perOption.D: Doubles the current instead of using $I^2 \propto 1/R$ at equal power.

questions.misconception: Thinking rectification changes the r.m.s. value, or using peak power as average power

explanation.body:
$I_{\max} = \dfrac{V_{\max}}{R} = \dfrac{150}{20} = 7.5\ \mathrm{A}$

perOption.B: Gives the peak current 7.5 A instead of the r.m.s. value.
perOption.C: Correct r.m.s. current, but uses peak power $I_0 V_0 = 1100\ \mathrm{W}$ instead of the mean.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires equating heating powers and taking the square root of the resistance ratio.
questions.misconception: Treating the steady current as the AC peak current.

explanation.body: The steady current dissipates power $I^2R$. The alternating current dissipates mean power $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2(R/2)$. Equating the two gives $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{2}I$.
